wa_big_snow_mountain_east_buttress.overview: A 10-pitch granite line up the crest of Big Snow Mountain's East Buttress above Hardscrabble Lake, first climbed with aid at NCCS III, 5.7, A1 in 1971 and later freed at 5.10 by Pete Doorish. A rarely repeated, semi-obscure Cascades classic on notably sound rock.
wa_big_snow_mountain_east_buttress.fa: Jeff Dial and Don Williamson, May 11, 1971

wa_crooked_thumb_peak_south_route.overview: Crooked Thumb Peak (8,129 ft) sits on the Northern Pickets crest exactly 0.5 mi south of Mount Challenger and 0.5 mi north of Phantom Peak, in North Cascades National Park's Whatcom County backcountry. The true summit is a striking, narrow 'fin' of white gneiss/granite only about 5 ft high — Fred and Helmy Beckey made the first ascent in 1940, and remarkably no one is recorded returning to sign the register until Phil Sharpe, Vic Josendal, and Warren Spickard's second ascent 18 years later in 1958 (Joe and Joan Firey made the third the following year). It remains one of the least-visited named summits in the Pickets.

wa_mount_fury_west_west_ridge.overview: West Peak carries the official USGS 'Mount Fury' benchmark and, via its long, loose connecting ridge from East Fury, is markedly harder than its twin summit — West Fury is routinely listed among the ten hardest Washington peaks by their easiest route. Precise modern surveying has found that East Fury is actually roughly 20 ft taller than West Fury (about 8,322 ft vs. roughly 8,300 ft), meaning the officially named summit is not the range's true high point, even though it remains the far more serious technical objective. The standard route climbs East Fury first, then follows a wild, exposed ridge traverse over three loose towers/gendarmes to reach West Fury's summit — typically adding a full 12-16+ hour day, with a real chance of a forced bivouac, onto an already multi-day Northern Pickets expedition.
wa_mount_fury_west_west_ridge.fa: Duke Watson, Phil Sharpe, Warren Spickard, Vic Josendal, and Maury Muzzy — August 19, 1958 (first ascent of West Peak)
